name: Unfiltered Tap Water
context: Municipal drinking water, straight from the tap
swap: A filter certified to NSF/ANSI 53 or 58 for the contaminant in your water
note: Quality varies widely by region. Common concerns are disinfection by-products, lead from old pipes, and trace PFAS. What a home filter removes depends on its type and on what it is certified to reduce — check the certifier’s listing for your contaminant.

name: Bottled Water (Plastic)
context: Single-use PET bottles
swap: Filtered tap water in a glass or steel bottle
note: Studies find microplastic and nanoplastic particles in most bottled water, shed from the plastic itself and worsened by heat and storage time.

name: Carbon-Filter Pitcher Water
context: Activated-carbon jug filter
note: Pitcher filters cut many chlorination by-products, but in a 2020 home study carbon filters of this kind removed only about 40–70% of PFAS. A filter works only while its cartridge is replaced on schedule.

name: Reverse-Osmosis Filtered Water
context: Under-sink RO system
note: In a 2020 home study, under-sink reverse-osmosis and two-stage filters removed nearly all the PFAS tested. Like any filter, it works only while its membrane and pre-filters are replaced on schedule; RO also sends about a gallon of water to the drain for every gallon it treats.

name: Untested Private Well Water
context: Private well, never tested
swap: Annual testing + a targeted filter
note: Wells aren't covered by public water rules. Arsenic, nitrates, bacteria and agricultural runoff are all possible and invisible without a test.

name: Scented Candles (Paraffin)
context: Burning fragranced paraffin candles indoors
swap: Unscented beeswax or soy, or none at all
note: Combustion releases fine particulate and VOCs; synthetic fragrance adds more. Ventilate, or skip the flame.

name: Plug-In Air Fresheners
context: Continuous synthetic-fragrance diffusers
swap: Open a window; simmer herbs; fix the odour source
note: They mask smell by adding phthalates and VOCs to the air you breathe all day. Real ventilation beats masking every time.

name: Unvented Gas Stove
context: Gas cooking with no range hood
swap: Vent to outside; run a hood; or induction
note: Gas burners emit nitrogen dioxide and fine particulate that can exceed outdoor limits in a closed kitchen. Always vent while cooking.

name: Wood-Burning Fireplace
context: Open indoor wood fires
swap: A sealed stove, or cleaner heating
note: Wood smoke is a major source of indoor PM2.5, linked to respiratory and cardiovascular harm. If you burn, use a sealed, well-drawing stove.

name: HEPA-Filtered Indoor Air
context: A true-HEPA air purifier sized to the room
note: One of the highest-value, lowest-effort exposure reductions: a correctly sized HEPA unit measurably cuts indoor PM2.5, pollen and many particulates.

name: Off-Gassing New Furniture
context: New pressed-wood furniture, mattresses, carpet
swap: Air out new items; choose low-VOC/CertiPUR
note: New composite wood and foams release formaldehyde and VOCs for weeks. Unwrap and ventilate before bringing them into bedrooms.

name: Burning Incense
context: Regular indoor incense
swap: Ventilate; essential-oil diffusion sparingly
note: Incense smoke can produce more fine particulate than cigarettes in a closed room. Reserve it for well-ventilated spaces.

name: Secondhand Cigarette Smoke
context: Living or working around indoor smoking
swap: A strictly smoke-free indoor environment
note: A confirmed human carcinogen with no safe level of exposure. Keeping all indoor spaces smoke-free is non-negotiable for detox load.

name: Nonstick (PTFE) Cookware
context: Teflon-type nonstick pans
swap: Cast iron or stainless steel
note: Scratched or overheated nonstick can shed PFAS-family compounds — the 'forever chemicals' that persist in the body and environment for years.

name: Cast Iron Cookware
context: Seasoned cast-iron pans
note: No synthetic coating to break down. A well-seasoned pan is naturally nonstick and can even add dietary iron.

name: Stainless Steel Cookware
context: 18/10 stainless pans and pots
note: Inert, durable, coating-free. The safe default for everyday high-heat cooking.

name: Uncoated Aluminum Cookware
context: Bare aluminum pots and foil with acidic food
swap: Anodized aluminum or stainless steel
note: Bare aluminum can leach into acidic foods like tomato sauce. Anodized or stainless removes the concern.

name: Plastic Cutting Boards
context: Cutting on soft plastic boards
swap: Wood or bamboo boards
note: Knife scoring sheds microplastic particles directly into your food. Wood is naturally antimicrobial and doesn't shed.

name: Conventional Strawberries
context: Non-organic strawberries (a 'Dirty Dozen' crop)
swap: Organic strawberries, or peel-heavy fruit instead
note: Consistently among the most pesticide-laden produce. This is a crop where buying organic meaningfully cuts residue.

name: Organic Strawberries
context: Certified-organic strawberries
note: Grown without synthetic pesticides. For high-residue crops, the organic version is a genuine exposure reduction.

name: Conventional Spinach
context: Non-organic leafy greens
swap: Organic greens; wash thoroughly
note: Leafy greens carry high pesticide residue because you eat the whole leaf. A strong candidate for buying organic.

name: Canned Food (BPA Lining)
context: Canned goods with epoxy linings
swap: Glass jars, cartons, or 'BPA-free' cans
note: BPA and its substitutes migrate from can linings into food, especially acidic and fatty contents. Choose glass or verified BPA-free packaging.

name: Large Predatory Fish
context: Tuna, swordfish, king mackerel, shark
swap: Small fish: sardines, anchovies, wild salmon
note: Mercury bioaccumulates up the food chain, concentrating in big long-lived predators. Small oily fish give the omega-3s with far less mercury.

name: Small Oily Fish (Sardines)
context: Sardines, anchovies, herring
note: Low on the food chain means low mercury, plus excellent omega-3s that support overall metabolic health.

name: Cruciferous Vegetables
context: Broccoli, cauliflower, cabbage, Brussels sprouts
note: Contain sulforaphane, which upregulates the body's own phase-II detoxification enzymes. One of the few foods that actively supports your detox systems.

name: Ultra-Processed Food
context: Packaged snacks, sodas, ready meals
swap: Whole, minimally processed foods
note: Carries additives, emulsifiers, and packaging-derived compounds, and displaces the fiber and phytonutrients your detox pathways rely on.

name: Charred Grilled Meat
context: Blackened, flame-grilled red meat
swap: Lower-temp cooking; trim char; marinate
note: High-heat charring forms heterocyclic amines and PAHs. Marinating, avoiding flare-ups and scraping off char cuts their formation.

name: White Rice (Arsenic)
context: Rice, especially for daily eaters and infants
swap: Rinse well, cook in excess water; vary grains
note: Rice takes up inorganic arsenic from soil and water. Rinsing and cooking in a high water-to-rice ratio removes a meaningful share.

name: Filtered Black Coffee
context: Paper-filtered coffee
note: Paper filtering removes cafestol; the drink itself is rich in antioxidants. A low-burden daily habit for most people.

name: Synthetic Fragrance / Perfume
context: 'Parfum' in perfume, lotion, and sprays
swap: Fragrance-free, or essential-oil scented sparingly
note: 'Fragrance' is an undisclosed mixture that often includes phthalates used to make scent linger. Fragrance-free is the simplest cut.

name: Aluminum Antiperspirant
context: Daily aluminum-based antiperspirant
swap: Aluminum-free deodorant if you prefer
note: Evidence of harm is weak and contested, but it's an easy swap for anyone who wants to reduce daily aluminum contact on skin.

name: Conventional Shampoo
context: Shampoo with parabens and harsh surfactants
swap: Paraben-free, simpler formulas
note: Leave-on and rinse-off products add up across the day. Simpler, paraben- and fragrance-free formulas reduce the cumulative load.

name: Nail Salon Products
context: Gel/acrylic nails, frequent salon visits
swap: '3-free/9-free' polish; ventilated salons
note: The 'toxic trio' — toluene, formaldehyde, DBP — plus solvent fumes make salons a real inhalation exposure. Choose ventilated shops and cleaner polishes.

name: Oxybenzone Sunscreen
context: Chemical sunscreens with oxybenzone
swap: Mineral (zinc oxide) sunscreen
note: Oxybenzone absorbs through skin and is an environmental concern. Mineral sunscreens protect just as well without it — and sunscreen itself stays essential.

name: Fragrance-Free Basic Skincare
context: Simple, unscented moisturizer and cleanser
note: Fewer ingredients means fewer unknowns. A short, fragrance-free routine is the low-burden default for skin.

name: Conventional All-Purpose Cleaner
context: Fragranced spray cleaners with QUATs/VOCs
swap: Simple vinegar/soap solutions; fragrance-free
note: Sprays aerosolize cleaning chemicals right into your breathing zone. Fragrance-free or DIY basics handle most household jobs.

name: Frequent Unventilated Bleach
context: Regular bleach use in closed rooms
swap: Ventilate; use only when needed; never mix
note: Bleach fumes irritate airways and form dangerous gases if mixed with ammonia or acids. Reserve it for real disinfection and open windows.

name: Dryer Sheets & Fabric Softener
context: Scented laundry softeners and sheets
swap: Wool dryer balls; skip softener
note: Coat fabric — and skin — in fragrance and quaternary compounds, then vent scented VOCs outdoors. Wool dryer balls do the softening job cleanly.

name: Vinegar & Baking Soda Cleaning
context: DIY non-toxic cleaning basics
note: Handles the majority of everyday cleaning with near-zero inhalation or residue burden. The low-cost, low-exposure baseline.

name: Home & Garden Pesticide Sprays
context: DIY insecticides and weed killers
swap: Physical controls; targeted, minimal use
note: Consumer pesticides drift indoors and settle into dust. Prefer traps, barriers and spot-treatment over broadcast spraying.

name: Stain-Resistant Textiles (PFAS)
context: 'Stain-proof' carpets, sofas, jackets
swap: Untreated fabrics; skip the stain-guard add-on
note: Stain and water repellency usually means PFAS coatings that shed into dust and never break down. Decline the optional stain treatment.

name: Vinyl (PVC) Shower Curtain
context: That 'new shower curtain' smell
swap: Fabric (polyester/cotton) or EVA curtain
note: The smell is phthalates off-gassing in a warm, humid room you breathe in daily. Fabric curtains wash and last without it.

name: Settled House Dust
context: Accumulated dust on floors and surfaces
swap: HEPA vacuum + damp dusting; doormats
note: House dust concentrates flame retardants, PFAS and phthalates — a bigger everyday exposure route than most people realize. Regular HEPA vacuuming genuinely lowers it.

name: Heating Food in Plastic
context: Microwaving or storing hot food in plastic
swap: Glass or ceramic for anything warm
note: Heat dramatically increases how much plastic and its additives migrate into food. Never microwave in plastic; transfer hot food to glass.

name: Plastic Wrap on Hot Food
context: Cling film touching warm, fatty food
swap: Let food cool; use a plate or beeswax wrap
note: Plasticizers migrate readily into hot, fatty foods. Cool food before covering, or use a lid instead of film.

name: Glass Food Storage
context: Glass containers for leftovers and meal prep
note: Inert, heat-safe and non-shedding. The single best swap to remove plastic-to-food migration from your kitchen.

name: Thermal Paper Receipts
context: Handling glossy receipts, especially with lotion
swap: Decline receipts; go digital; wash hands
note: The coating is often BPA/BPS, absorbed through skin — more so with hand sanitizer or lotion on. Skip the paper receipt when you can.

name: Hot Greasy Takeout Containers
context: Molded-fiber bowls and grease-proof wrappers
swap: Transfer food out; cook at home more often
note: Grease-resistant food packaging is a known PFAS source, and hot food speeds migration. Move takeout onto a plate promptly.

name: Canned & Reused Plastic Bottles
context: Refilling single-use bottles; canned drinks
swap: A dedicated steel or glass reusable
note: Single-use bottles aren't built for reuse — wear and heat increase leaching and bacterial growth. A proper reusable is cleaner and cheaper over time.

name: Roadside & Traffic Air
context: Living, running, or cycling next to heavy traffic
swap: Exercise away from traffic; filter home air
note: Traffic exhaust delivers PM2.5, benzene and ultrafine particles. Move workouts to parks and back streets, and filter indoor air near busy roads.

name: Regular Sauna Use
context: Consistent sauna or heat bathing
note: Associated with cardiovascular benefits and supports the body's natural processes through heat adaptation and sweating. Hydrate well and listen to your body.

name: New-Car Interior Off-Gassing
context: That 'new car smell'
swap: Ventilate; park in shade; air it out for weeks
note: The smell is VOCs and flame retardants off-gassing from plastics and adhesives, worse in heat. Ventilate generously for the first months.

name: Dry-Cleaned Clothes (Perc)
context: Traditional perchloroethylene dry cleaning
swap: Air out garments; choose 'green' cleaners
note: Perc is a probable carcinogen that lingers in freshly cleaned fabric. Air garments outside the bag before wearing, or use wet/green cleaners.

name: Untested Basement Radon
context: Lower-floor living space, never tested for radon
swap: A cheap radon test kit, then mitigate if high
note: Radon is the second-leading cause of lung cancer and is completely invisible. A one-time test is among the highest-value things on this whole list.

name: Regular Exercise & Sweat
context: Consistent physical activity
note: Supports circulation, lymphatic flow and overall metabolic health — the foundation your body's own clearance systems run on. Not a 'detox' shortcut, but the real thing.

name: Microwave Popcorn Bags
context: The grease-proof lining of microwave popcorn bags
swap: Air-pop plain kernels in a pot or a plain paper bag
note: The non-stick lining has historically used PFAS 'forever chemicals' that can migrate into the oil and popcorn when heated. Loose kernels cost less and skip the coating entirely.

name: Plastic Tea Bags
context: Pyramid-style mesh tea bags steeped in boiling water
swap: Loose-leaf tea with a stainless-steel infuser, or unbleached paper bags
note: Nylon and PET mesh bags can shed microplastics into hot water. Loose leaf or paper bags avoid the plastic and often taste better.

name: Dark Chocolate (Heavy Metals)
context: Cocoa-heavy dark chocolate eaten regularly
swap: Enjoy in moderation and favour brands that publish third-party heavy-metal testing
note: Cocoa can carry trace cadmium and lead from soil and processing. Occasional squares are fine; the concern is large daily amounts, especially for children.

name: Farmed Salmon
context: Conventionally farmed Atlantic salmon
swap: Wild-caught salmon, or smaller oily fish like sardines and mackerel
note: Farmed fish can carry more of certain fat-soluble contaminants than wild. It is still a good protein source — variety and smaller species lower the load.

name: Mothballs (Naphthalene)
context: Naphthalene or paradichlorobenzene mothballs in closets
swap: Cedar blocks, lavender sachets, or sealed garment bags
note: Mothballs slowly sublimate into a gas you breathe in enclosed spaces. Physical barriers and natural deterrents protect clothes without the fumes.

name: Vinyl (PVC) Flooring
context: Flexible vinyl plank or sheet flooring
swap: Sealed hardwood, tile, or verified phthalate-free flooring
note: Soft PVC flooring can off-gas phthalate plasticisers, especially when new and warm. Hard, inert surfaces avoid the issue.

name: Antibacterial Soap (Triclosan)
context: Hand and body washes marketed as antibacterial
swap: Plain soap and water — equally effective for everyday handwashing
note: Triclosan is a persistent antimicrobial with no proven benefit over plain soap for home use, and it ends up in waterways. Regulators have already pulled it from many products.

name: Talc-Based Body Powder
context: Loose talcum powder used on skin
swap: Cornstarch-based powder
note: The concern is possible asbestos contamination in mined talc and inhalation of fine particles. Cornstarch powders sidestep both.

name: Permanent Hair Dye
context: Oxidative permanent hair colour applied at home or salon
swap: Henna, semi-permanent dyes, or less frequent application in a ventilated space
note: Permanent dyes contain aromatic amines absorbed through the scalp. Spacing out applications and good ventilation reduce the dose.

name: Old Lead Paint
context: Deteriorating paint in homes built before the late 1970s
swap: Professional lead-safe remediation — never dry-sand it yourself
note: Lead paint dust is one of the most serious avoidable household exposures, especially for young children. Disturbing it wrong makes it far worse; use certified remediation.

name: Plastic Children's Toys
context: Soft plastic toys, especially older or imported ones
swap: Wood, silicone, or certified phthalate-free toys
note: Soft plastics can contain phthalates that children mouth and handle. Modern certified toys limit these; the risk is mostly older or unregulated imports.

name: Chlorinated Shower Water
context: Hot showers in chlorinated municipal water
swap: Shorter showers
note: Hot showers release chloroform and other disinfection by-products into the air you breathe, and some are absorbed through the skin. In a volunteer study, one of them, bromodichloromethane, fell to near undetectable blood levels within a day of skin exposure.

name: Black Plastic Kitchen Utensils
context: Black nylon/plastic spatulas and serving spoons
swap: Stainless steel or solid wood utensils
note: Some black plastic kitchenware is made from recycled electronic plastic and can carry brominated flame retardants that migrate into hot food. Metal or wood avoids the issue.

name: Nonstick Air Fryer Basket
context: PTFE-coated air fryer baskets and trays
swap: A stainless-steel or ceramic-coated basket
note: High-heat cooking on scratched PTFE coatings can release fumes and shed particles. Uncoated stainless or a ceramic liner sidesteps the fluorinated coating.

name: Melamine Dishware
context: Melamine plates and bowls used with hot food
swap: Glass, ceramic or stainless dishware
note: Melamine can migrate from the dish into hot, acidic or microwaved food. It is fine for cold use, but keep it away from heat, or switch to glass.

name: Silicone Bakeware
context: Food-grade silicone moulds and mats
note: Good-quality food-grade silicone is stable and low-migration at normal baking temperatures. Choose platinum-cured silicone and avoid cheap fillers for the cleanest option.

name: Conventional Apples
context: Non-organic apples eaten with skin
swap: Organic apples, or wash and peel
note: Apples rank high on pesticide-residue testing because residues concentrate in the skin. Washing helps, peeling helps more, and organic avoids most of it.

name: Conventional Grapes
context: Non-organic table grapes
swap: Organic grapes, or a thorough rinse
note: Grapes routinely show multiple pesticide residues on residue-monitoring lists. A good rinse cuts surface residue; organic avoids most of it.

name: Deli Meats
context: Processed sliced ham, salami and cured meats
swap: Fresh-roasted meat you slice yourself
note: Processed meats are classified as a group 1 carcinogen, driven partly by nitrite-formed nitrosamines. Occasional use is one thing; daily deli sandwiches add up.

name: Canned Tuna
context: Albacore/white canned tuna eaten frequently
swap: Light skipjack tuna or small oily fish like sardines
note: Larger tuna accumulate methylmercury, which builds up in the body. Choosing smaller 'light' tuna or sardines keeps the omega-3s with far less mercury.

name: Protein Powder
context: Daily protein-powder shakes
swap: A third-party heavy-metal-tested powder, or whole-food protein
note: Independent testing has found lead, cadmium and arsenic in some protein powders, especially plant and chocolate varieties. Look for published heavy-metal testing.

name: Conventional Makeup (PFAS)
context: Long-wear foundation, mascara and lipstick
swap: Cosmetics labelled PFAS-free
note: Studies have detected PFAS 'forever chemicals' in many long-wear and waterproof cosmetics, applied daily right on the skin. PFAS-free lines avoid them.

name: Scented Body Wash
context: Fragranced shower gels and washes
swap: A fragrance-free or essential-oil-only wash
note: 'Fragrance' can hide phthalates used to make scent last. You rinse it off, but daily whole-body use adds up — fragrance-free removes the guesswork.

name: Chemical Hair Relaxers
context: Chemical straightening and relaxer treatments
swap: Skip chemical straightening; heat-style sparingly
note: Large studies link frequent chemical hair-straightener use to hormone-related health risks, and some release formaldehyde. Reducing frequency lowers the exposure.

name: Conventional Body Lotion
context: Fragranced lotions with parabens
swap: A fragrance-free, paraben-free lotion
note: Applied over a large skin area daily, paraben-and-fragrance lotions are a steady low-level exposure. Simple fragrance-free formulas do the same job.

name: PFAS-Coated Dental Floss
context: Slick PTFE/PFAS-coated 'glide' floss
swap: Uncoated or natural-wax floss
note: Some smooth 'glide' flosses are PTFE-based, and research has associated their use with higher PFAS levels. Plain waxed floss works just as well.

name: Flame-Retardant Furniture Foam
context: Older upholstered sofas and chairs with FR foam
swap: Furniture labelled free of added flame retardants (TB117-2013)
note: Older upholstered foam often contains persistent flame retardants that migrate into house dust. Newer 'no added flame retardants' labelling avoids them.

name: Conventional Mattress
context: New synthetic mattress off-gassing
swap: A CertiPUR-US or GOTS/GOLS-certified mattress; air out new ones
note: You spend a third of your life in contact with it, and new synthetic mattresses can off-gas VOCs and carry flame retardants. Certified low-emission foam or natural latex reduces both.

name: New Carpet
context: Freshly installed wall-to-wall carpet
swap: Low-VOC hard flooring or untreated wool rugs
note: New carpet can off-gas VOCs and often carries PFAS-based stain treatment that ends up in house dust. Hard flooring or untreated natural fibres avoids the stain chemistry.

name: Antibacterial Wipes
context: Quat-based disinfecting wipes used daily
swap: Plain soap and water, or plant-based cleaners
note: Quaternary ammonium 'quat' disinfectants are respiratory irritants and are overkill for everyday surfaces. Soap and water handles most home cleaning.

name: Pressed-Wood Furniture
context: Particleboard and MDF furniture off-gassing
swap: Solid wood or CARB2 / formaldehyde-free rated pieces
note: Particleboard and MDF glues can off-gas formaldehyde, a known irritant and carcinogen, for months. Solid wood or low-emission certified board reduces it.

name: Polyester Clothing
context: Synthetic fabrics that shed microfibres
swap: Natural fibres — cotton, wool, linen; a microfibre laundry bag
note: Synthetic clothing sheds plastic microfibres in the wash and through wear, adding to microplastic exposure. Natural fibres and a filter bag cut the shedding.

name: Disposable Coffee Cups
context: Plastic-lined paper cups for hot drinks
swap: A reusable ceramic or stainless cup
note: The thin plastic lining that makes paper cups waterproof can shed microplastic particles into hot liquid. A reusable cup avoids the daily dose.

name: Vinyl (PVC) Yoga Mat
context: Soft PVC exercise and yoga mats
swap: A TPE, cork or natural-rubber mat
note: Flexible PVC mats can contain phthalate plasticisers and give off that 'new plastic' smell. TPE, cork or rubber mats skip the PVC chemistry.

name: Old Lead Plumbing
context: Lead service lines or old solder in home plumbing
swap: Test the water, use a filter certified to NSF/ANSI 53 for lead, and replace the lead line
note: Lead pipes and solder can leach lead into tap water, and harm has been measured even at low blood-lead levels. Have the water tested, and use a filter certified to NSF/ANSI 53 for lead until the line is replaced.

name: Chlorinated Pool Water
context: Frequent indoor chlorinated-pool swimming
swap: Rinse before and after; well-ventilated or saltwater pools
note: Chlorine reacts with sweat and skin oils to form disinfection by-products you absorb and inhale, worst in poorly ventilated indoor pools. Showering first and good ventilation help.

name: Wildfire Smoke
context: Fine-particle smoke during wildfire season
swap: HEPA air purifier indoors; a fitted N95 outdoors
note: Wildfire smoke is loaded with fine PM2.5 that reaches deep into the lungs. On smoky days, a HEPA purifier indoors and a fitted N95 outdoors cut what you breathe in.

name: Aluminum Foil (Cooking)
context: Wrapping or cooking hot, acidic food in foil
swap: Parchment paper, or cook in a glass or ceramic dish
note: Small amounts of aluminum migrate into food, more so with heat and acidic ingredients like tomato or lemon. Everyday amounts are generally considered low-risk, but you can avoid the transfer entirely with an inert surface.

name: Plastic Coffee Pods (K-Cups)
context: Single-serve plastic pods brewed with near-boiling water
swap: A reusable stainless-steel pod, or a French press or moka pot
note: Forcing hot water through a thin plastic pod can release microplastics and, from some plastics, trace additives. A steel filter avoids the disposable plastic entirely.

name: Fabric Protector Spray (PFAS)
context: Aftermarket stain-repellent sprays for furniture, shoes and carpet
swap: Skip the spray; choose untreated natural-fibre textiles and blot spills promptly
note: Many stain and water repellents rely on PFAS, the persistent fluorinated compounds that build up in the body and environment. Aerosol application also means you inhale the mist.

name: Glyphosate Weed Killer
context: Home garden and lawn herbicide use
swap: Manual weeding, mulching, or a vinegar-based spot herbicide
note: Glyphosate residues are widely detected and its hazard classification is debated by regulators. For home use, non-chemical weed control removes the exposure and the drift onto edible plants.

name: DEET Insect Repellent
context: Skin-applied mosquito and tick repellent
swap: Apply to clothing rather than skin, or use a picaridin repellent
note: DEET is registered and effective at preventing insect-borne disease, and that protection often outweighs the exposure. To reduce contact, use the lowest effective concentration and wash it off once indoors.

name: Conventional Kale
context: Non-organic kale, a frequent pesticide-residue crop
swap: Organic kale, or wash and soak thoroughly before eating
note: Leafy greens like kale regularly appear high on pesticide-residue rankings. The vegetable itself is nutritious — the exposure is the residue, which washing and organic sourcing reduce.

name: Conventional Peaches
context: Non-organic peaches and nectarines
swap: Organic peaches, or peel and wash conventional ones
note: Soft-skinned stone fruit tends to carry more surface pesticide residue. Choosing organic or peeling reduces the residue you consume without giving up the fruit.

name: Microwave Frozen Meals (Plastic Tray)
context: Heating a ready meal in its plastic tray or film
swap: Transfer the food to a glass or ceramic dish before microwaving
note: Microwaving in plastic is one of the biggest drivers of chemical and microplastic migration into food, because heat accelerates the transfer. Moving the food to glass first avoids it.

name: Fast-Food Wrappers (PFAS)
context: Grease-resistant wrappers, bags and boxes for hot food
swap: Unwrap greasy food promptly, or cook the same meals at home
note: Grease-proof food packaging has often been treated with PFAS, which can migrate into hot, oily food. Getting the food out of the wrapper quickly limits the contact time.

name: Turmeric Supplements (Lead)
context: Bulk or imported turmeric powder and capsules
swap: Buy turmeric from brands that publish heavy-metal testing
note: Some turmeric has been adulterated with lead-based colourant to brighten it, a documented source of lead exposure. Third-party-tested brands avoid the problem.

name: Ground Cinnamon (Lead)
context: Some imported ground cinnamon and cinnamon products
swap: Use Ceylon cinnamon from tested, reputable brands
note: Recent recalls found elevated lead in certain cinnamon and cinnamon-flavoured products. The spice in normal amounts is fine — the concern is contamination in specific low-quality supply chains.

name: Aerosol Dry Shampoo (Benzene)
context: Spray-can dry shampoo used near the scalp
swap: A non-aerosol powder dry shampoo, or simply washing your hair
note: Testing has found benzene, a known carcinogen, contaminating some aerosol dry shampoos from the propellant. Powder formats avoid both the contaminant and the inhaled mist.

name: Aerosol Sunscreen Spray (Benzene)
context: Spray sunscreens found to contain benzene contamination
swap: A mineral (zinc oxide) lotion sunscreen
note: Several spray sunscreens were recalled after benzene was detected. Sun protection still matters — a lotion, especially a mineral one, gives the protection without the propellant and contamination risk.

name: Conventional Tampons
context: Scented or conventional cotton/rayon menstrual products
swap: Unscented organic-cotton products, or a medical-grade silicone cup
note: Menstrual products contact absorptive tissue, and studies have detected fragrance chemicals and trace metals in some. Unscented, tested materials reduce that contact exposure.

name: Baby Food Pouches (Heavy Metals)
context: Commercial infant purees, especially rice-based ones
swap: Vary grains away from rice and serve fresh homemade purees
note: Investigations have found arsenic, lead and cadmium in some commercial baby foods, with rice-based products highest. Varying ingredients and making purees at home lowers the cumulative intake.

name: Laundry Detergent (1,4-Dioxane)
context: Conventional and heavily fragranced laundry detergents
swap: A fragrance-free detergent screened for 1,4-dioxane
note: Some detergents contain 1,4-dioxane, a manufacturing by-product, plus fragrance allergens that linger on clothes against the skin. Certified fragrance-free products reduce both.

name: Artificial Turf (Crumb Rubber)
context: Synthetic sports and play surfaces with rubber infill
swap: Natural grass where possible, and wash hands after play
note: Crumb-rubber infill and turf fibres can contain PFAS, PAHs and metals. Skin and hand-to-mouth contact are the main routes, so washing up after use reduces it.

name: Garden Hose Water
context: Drinking from or filling bottles with a standard garden hose
swap: A hose labelled drinking-water-safe (lead-free), and let it run first
note: Ordinary hoses can leach lead, BPA and phthalates, especially after sitting in the sun. A drinking-water-rated hose and flushing the warm water first avoid most of it.

name: Pressure-Treated Wood
context: Chemically treated lumber for decks, raised beds and play sets
swap: Seal it, or use untreated cedar or composite for garden and play surfaces
note: Older pressure-treated wood used arsenic-based preservative; newer types use copper compounds that can still leach. Sealing the wood or choosing untreated material limits skin and soil contact.

name: Aerosol Air Freshener Spray
context: Spray-can room and fabric fresheners
swap: Open a window, or simmer citrus peel and herbs
note: Aerosol fresheners release VOCs and often phthalates as fragrance carriers, which you then inhale in an enclosed room. Ventilation addresses odour at the source rather than masking it.

name: Plastic Baby Bottles (Heated)
context: Polypropylene bottles used for hot formula preparation
swap: Glass or stainless-steel bottles, and cool water before it touches plastic
note: Research published in Nature Food found polypropylene infant bottles release very large numbers of microplastic particles when formula is prepared at high temperature, with release rising sharply with water temperature. Preparing in a non-plastic vessel and cooling before transfer lowers release substantially.

name: Paper & Bamboo Drinking Straws
context: Plastic-free straws marketed as the eco option
swap: Stainless-steel or glass straws, or simply no straw
note: A Belgian survey published in Food Additives & Contaminants detected PFAS in the majority of paper and bamboo straws tested — often at higher rates than in plastic ones, because the coating that makes them water-resistant is itself fluorinated. Reusable metal or glass avoids the coating question entirely.

name: Unlined Copper Cookware
context: Bare copper pots in contact with acidic food
swap: Tin- or stainless-lined copper, or plain stainless steel
note: Copper leaches readily into acidic foods, which is why food-safety codes restrict bare copper surfaces from contacting acidic ingredients. Lined copper keeps the heat-conduction benefit without the direct food contact.

name: Imported Glazed Ceramic Dishware
context: Traditional or artisanal glazed pottery used for food
swap: Ceramics certified lead-free for food use, or plain porcelain and glass
note: Health agencies have repeatedly documented lead leaching from traditional glazed pottery, particularly when it holds acidic or hot food. Decorative pieces are not always fired to food-safe standards; keep unverified glazed pottery ornamental.

name: Decorated Vintage Glassware
context: Enamelled or painted drinking glasses and dishes
swap: Undecorated plain glass, or keep painted pieces for display only
note: Analytical work published in Science of the Total Environment found lead and cadmium in the enamelled decoration on a large share of drinking glasses tested, including new items. The glass itself is inert — the concern is the exterior paint, especially where it meets the rim.

name: Unvented Portable Kerosene Heater
context: Flueless kerosene or paraffin space heaters
swap: Vented heating, or electric heaters with a window cracked
note: Any unvented combustion appliance puts its entire exhaust — nitrogen dioxide, carbon monoxide and fine particles — into the room it is heating. Vented or electric heating removes the combustion products from the indoor air entirely.

name: 3D Printer Fumes
context: Desktop filament printers running in an unventilated room
swap: An enclosed printer vented outside, or a HEPA-and-carbon enclosure
note: Melting filament emits ultrafine particles and VOCs, with emission rates varying widely by material — ABS is consistently measured higher than PLA. Enclosing and venting the printer, or running it in a room you are not sitting in, addresses most of it.

name: Laser Printer Toner Emissions
context: Office laser printers on or beside a desk
swap: Site the printer away from desks in a ventilated space
note: Work published in Environmental Science & Technology found some laser printers emit substantial ultrafine particles during printing, driven by the hot fuser. Distance and ventilation are the practical levers, since emission is highest right at the machine.

name: Scented Wax Melts
context: Flame-free warmers marketed as a cleaner alternative to candles
swap: Unscented warmers, or ventilation instead of fragrance
note: Because they are flameless, wax melts are often assumed to be the clean option. Research from Purdue published in Environmental Science & Technology Letters found they release high levels of fragrance terpenes that react with indoor ozone to form nanoparticles, at levels comparable to combustion sources.

name: Ultrasonic Humidifier (Tap Water)
context: Cool-mist humidifiers filled straight from the tap
swap: Distilled or demineralised water, emptied and cleaned between uses
note: Ultrasonic units aerosolise whatever is in the tank — dissolved minerals become the fine white dust that settles on surfaces, and a standing tank can grow microbial films. Distilled water and routine cleaning address both.

name: Damp & Mould in the Home
context: Persistent damp, condensation or visible mould growth
swap: Fix the moisture source, ventilate, and keep humidity below 50%
note: WHO guidance on indoor air quality treats persistent indoor damp as a well-established respiratory irritant. Remediation works on the water, not the mould — cleaning visible growth without fixing the moisture source simply lets it return.

name: Nail Polish (Triphenyl Phosphate)
context: Conventional polish containing TPHP as a plasticiser
swap: Polish labelled TPHP-free, and apply in a ventilated room
note: A study in Environment International measured a clear rise in a TPHP metabolite in urine after participants painted their nails, showing the plasticiser is absorbed rather than staying on the surface. TPHP-free formulations are now widely available and labelled.

name: Keratin Hair Smoothing Treatments
context: Salon smoothing systems that release formaldehyde when heated
swap: Formaldehyde-free smoothing systems, or skip the treatment
note: Occupational safety regulators issued hazard alerts after air testing found formaldehyde released during these treatments, including from products labelled formaldehyde-free. Salon workers carry the heaviest exposure because it is repeated daily.

name: Gel Manicure UV Lamps
context: UV curing lamps used to set gel polish
swap: UV-protective fingerless gloves, or regular polish
note: These lamps emit UVA. Laboratory work published in Nature Communications documented DNA damage in human cells exposed to gel-lamp radiation. Fingerless UV gloves are an inexpensive way to keep the exposure off the skin while still curing the polish.

name: Recalled Hand Sanitiser (Benzene & Methanol)
context: Gel sanitisers from unverified manufacturers
swap: Soap and water where available; check recall lists for your brand
note: Regulators issued extensive recalls after testing found methanol substituted for ethanol in some sanitisers, and independent laboratory testing later flagged benzene contamination in specific batches. Washing with soap and water avoids the supply-chain question altogether.

name: Infant Rice Cereal (Inorganic Arsenic)
context: Single-grain rice cereal as a first food
swap: Rotate in oat, barley and multigrain cereals
note: Rice takes up more inorganic arsenic from soil and water than other grains, and regulators set a specific action level for infant rice cereal because infants eat a large amount relative to body weight. Varying the grain is the straightforward move.

name: Ayurvedic Herbal Supplements
context: Imported traditional herbal remedies
swap: Third-party tested supplements carrying a USP or NSF mark
note: Testing published in JAMA found detectable lead, mercury or arsenic in roughly one in five Ayurvedic products purchased in the United States, including products bought online. Independent third-party certification is the practical filter.

name: Herbal Teas (Pyrrolizidine Alkaloids)
context: Botanical infusions drunk daily from one source
swap: Rotate varieties and brands rather than drinking one blend daily
note: European food-safety surveys have found pyrrolizidine alkaloids in herbal and tea products, arriving as weed contamination during harvest rather than from the named plant. Rotating what you drink keeps any single contaminated source from becoming a daily habit.

name: Hijiki Seaweed
context: A specific sea vegetable used in Japanese cooking
swap: Nori, wakame or kombu, which do not carry the same finding
note: Food-safety agencies in several countries advise against eating hijiki specifically, after testing found inorganic arsenic at levels far above other edible seaweeds. This is unusual among sea vegetables — the common alternatives are not implicated.

name: Sea Salt (Microplastics)
context: Salt evaporated from seawater
swap: Mined rock salt, which does not pass through seawater
note: Multiple international surveys have detected microplastic particles in the large majority of sea salt brands tested, tracking the plastic load of the source water. Rock salt comes from ancient deposits and consistently tests lower.

name: Harvested Rainwater
context: Roof-collected rainwater used for drinking
swap: Drink mains water rather than untreated roof rainwater
note: Rain carries PFAS: a 2022 global analysis in Environmental Science & Technology found PFOA and PFOS in rainwater often far above US EPA drinking-water advisory levels, and 28% of roof-harvested samples in an Arizona study exceeded the then 70 ng/L advisory. Roofs and tanks add their own: 1–4% of 100 Australian household tanks exceeded drinking-water health values for metals.

name: Idling a Vehicle in an Attached Garage
context: Warming up or running an engine with the garage door closed
swap: Reverse out first, and never run an engine in a closed garage
note: Exhaust in an attached garage carries carbon monoxide and benzene into the living space through the shared wall, and concentrations build quickly in an enclosed space. Backing out before starting removes the exposure completely and costs nothing.

name: Conventional Blueberries
context: Non-organic fresh or frozen blueberries
swap: Organic blueberries, or a good rinse before eating
note: EWG added blueberries to its Dirty Dozen after USDA testing found residues of organophosphate insecticides on a large share of samples. Organic removes the concern, and even conventional berries stay a nutritious choice once washed.

name: Conventional Green Beans
context: Non-organic fresh or frozen green beans
swap: Organic green beans, or wash conventional ones well
note: USDA sampling behind EWG's Dirty Dozen found residues of acephate — an insecticide the EPA banned on the crop decades ago — on some conventional green beans. Buying organic sidesteps it entirely.

name: Conventional Bell Peppers
context: Non-organic sweet bell peppers
swap: Organic peppers, or wash and peel where practical
note: Peppers sit high on EWG's Dirty Dozen because their thin skin retains multiple pesticide residues per sample. They are worth eating; buying the organic version is the clean upgrade.

name: Conventional Celery
context: Non-organic celery stalks
swap: Organic celery
note: Celery is a perennial Dirty Dozen entry: with no protective peel, USDA tests routinely find several pesticide residues on a single stalk. Organic is the straightforward swap.

name: Conventional Cherries
context: Non-organic fresh cherries
swap: Organic cherries, or wash thoroughly
note: Cherries appear on EWG's Dirty Dozen, with USDA testing detecting organophosphate residues on many samples. A thorough rinse helps; organic removes the issue.

name: Conventional Potatoes
context: Non-organic potatoes
swap: Organic potatoes, or peel before cooking
note: Conventional potatoes are treated with chlorpropham, a sprout-inhibitor found on the skin of many samples. Because potatoes are eaten so often, the cumulative exposure adds up — peeling or buying organic reduces it.

name: Skin-Lightening Creams (Mercury)
context: Imported or unregulated skin-whitening and anti-aging creams
swap: Avoid entirely; use mercury-free vitamin C or niacinamide brighteners
note: The FDA and EPA warn that some imported skin-lightening creams contain mercury at dangerous levels, which absorbs through skin and accumulates in the body and nervous system. There is no safe use — check labels for 'mercurous chloride', 'calomel' or 'mercurio' and discard them.

name: Kohl / Kajal Eyeliner (Lead)
context: Traditional kohl, kajal, surma or tiro eye cosmetics
swap: FDA-approved eyeliner from a regulated brand
note: The FDA has repeatedly warned that traditional kohl and kajal can be largely lead salts, and their use near the eye is linked to raised blood-lead levels, especially in children. Only cosmetics with an FDA-approved colour additive list are safe substitutes.

name: Imported Candy (Lead)
context: Certain imported tamarind, chili or clay-based sweets
swap: Reputable domestic brands; avoid candies in unlabeled or ceramic wrappers
note: California and the FDA have documented lead in some imported candies, traced to chili powder, tamarind and the ink or ceramic of the wrapper. Children are most vulnerable; choosing regulated brands avoids the risk.

name: Vaping / E-Cigarette Aerosol
context: Inhaling and exhaling e-cigarette vapour indoors
swap: Quit vaping; seek nicotine-cessation support
note: E-cigarette aerosol is not just water vapour: peer-reviewed analyses find heavy metals such as lead, nickel and chromium leached from the coil, plus formaldehyde and fine particulate. Secondhand vapour exposes bystanders too.

name: Vinyl Tablecloth (Phthalates & Lead)
context: Flexible PVC tablecloths and placemats
swap: Cotton, linen, or PEVA/EVA tablecloths
note: Independent testing has found flexible vinyl tablecloths that contain phthalate plasticizers and, in some products, lead used as a stabilizer — both of which can transfer to hands and food. Natural-fibre or PVC-free covers avoid it.

name: Faux-Leather (PVC) Furniture
context: Sofas and chairs upholstered in vinyl 'bonded leather'
swap: Real leather, wool, or polyurethane (PU) upholstery
note: Most inexpensive faux leather is PVC softened with phthalate plasticizers that migrate out and settle into house dust over the years you own the piece. Genuine leather, wool or PU alternatives skip the softeners.

name: Costume Jewelry (Lead & Cadmium)
context: Cheap metal fashion jewelry and children's trinkets
swap: Solid stainless steel, titanium, or precious metals
note: CPSC recalls and independent testing regularly find high levels of lead and cadmium in low-cost metal jewelry, a hazard mainly through skin contact and, for children, mouthing. Stainless steel, titanium or solid gold/silver are inert.

name: Ceramic-Coated Nonstick Pans
context: Sol-gel 'ceramic' nonstick cookware marketed as PFAS-free
swap: Bare cast iron or stainless steel
note: Ceramic nonstick avoids PTFE, which is a genuine plus, but the thin sol-gel coating wears off within a year or two and its full nanoparticle composition is rarely disclosed. Cast iron and stainless last for decades with nothing to shed.

name: Bentonite Clay Detox Products (Lead)
context: Edible 'detox' clay powders and cleanses
swap: Skip clay cleanses; support your body's own clearance
note: The FDA has warned that some edible bentonite clay 'detox' products contain elevated lead, which the clay draws from its geological source. Ironically, a product sold to remove toxins can add one — and there is no evidence it detoxes anything.

name: Chewing Gum (Microplastics)
context: Conventional gum made with a synthetic polymer base
swap: Natural chicle-based gum, or skip gum
note: The 'gum base' in most conventional chewing gum is synthetic rubber — essentially plastic. A 2025 laboratory study reported that chewing a single piece can release hundreds to thousands of microplastic particles into saliva. Natural chicle gum avoids the synthetic base.

name: Conventional Pears
context: Non-organic pears, eaten with the skin
swap: Organic pears, or wash and peel conventional ones
note: Pears appear on the EWG Dirty Dozen because residues of several pesticides are commonly detected. Washing helps and peeling removes more, though it also removes fiber.

name: Conventional Nectarines
context: Non-organic nectarines with edible skin
swap: Organic nectarines, or thorough washing
note: A recurring Dirty Dozen fruit: the thin, edible skin holds detectable multi-pesticide residues. Buying organic for the ones you eat most is a reasonable, budget-aware move.

name: Canned Tomatoes (BPA-Lined)
context: Acidic canned tomatoes in a can with epoxy lining
swap: Tomatoes in glass jars or Tetra cartons, or fresh
note: Acidity increases how much bisphenol migrates from an epoxy can lining into the food. Glass or carton packaging sidesteps the lining entirely.

name: Swordfish (High Mercury)
context: A large, long-lived predatory fish high on the food chain
swap: Lower-mercury fish like salmon, sardines or trout
note: Swordfish is on the FDA/EPA 'avoid' list for its high methylmercury content, which accumulates in the body. Pregnant people and young children are advised to skip it.

name: Rice-Based Drinks (Arsenic)
context: Rice milk used as a dairy alternative
swap: Oat, soy or pea-protein milk
note: Rice concentrates inorganic arsenic from soil and water. UK and other agencies advise that young children in particular should not rely on rice drinks; other plant milks avoid the issue.

name: Imported Farmed Shrimp
context: Cheap imported farmed shrimp of uncertain provenance
swap: Certified (ASC/BAP) or wild-caught shrimp
note: Some imported farmed shrimp has been flagged for antibiotic and contaminant residues due to weak oversight. Certification schemes and known wild sources reduce that uncertainty.

name: Instant Noodle Cups (Boiling Water in Plastic)
context: Pouring boiling water directly into a polystyrene or plastic-lined cup
swap: Cook the noodles in a pot and eat from a ceramic bowl
note: Boiling water in a plastic or foam cup increases microplastic and chemical migration into the broth. Transferring to a pot and bowl avoids heating the plastic.

name: Lipstick (Lead & Metals)
context: Colour lipstick reapplied throughout the day
swap: Fewer reapplications and brands that publish metal-testing
note: FDA surveys have detected trace lead and other metals in many lipsticks. Because lipstick is worn on the lips and partly ingested, frequency of reapplication is the main lever.

name: Aerosol Hair Spray (VOCs)
context: Propellant hair spray used in an unventilated bathroom
swap: A non-aerosol pump spray, used with the door open
note: Aerosols create a fine, easily inhaled mist of solvents and propellants. A pump product and good ventilation cut how much you breathe in.

name: Petroleum-Based Lip Balm
context: Mineral-oil / petrolatum lip balm applied and ingested daily
swap: Beeswax or plant-oil balms from refined sources
note: Poorly refined mineral oils can carry aromatic hydrocarbon impurities, and lip products are partly swallowed. Well-made plant- or beeswax-based balms avoid the concern.

name: Scented Menstrual Pads
context: Fragranced disposable pads worn against sensitive tissue
swap: Fragrance-free or organic-cotton pads and tampons
note: Added fragrance can include undisclosed phthalates and irritants placed against thin, absorptive skin. Fragrance-free products remove an exposure that serves no functional purpose.

name: Octinoxate Sunscreen
context: A chemical UV filter absorbed through skin
swap: A mineral (zinc oxide) sunscreen
note: Octinoxate is a chemical filter with hormone-disruption questions and measurable skin absorption. Mineral zinc-oxide sunscreens sit on the skin and avoid the issue while still protecting you — sun protection still matters.

name: Coloured Tattoo Ink (Metals & PAHs)
context: Pigmented tattoo inks deposited permanently in the skin
swap: A reputable artist using REACH-compliant, disclosed inks
note: Some coloured inks contain heavy metals and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, and the pigment stays in skin and lymph nodes for life. Choosing a professional using regulated inks reduces what goes in.

name: Fresh Latex Paint (VOCs)
context: Newly painted interior walls off-gassing solvents
swap: Zero- or low-VOC paint, with windows open while it cures
note: Conventional paint releases volatile organic compounds for days to weeks after application. Zero-VOC formulas plus ventilation dramatically cut what you breathe.

name: Vinyl Mini-Blinds (Lead Dust)
context: Imported PVC window blinds that degrade in sunlight
swap: Aluminium, wood, or certified lead-free blinds
note: Older or imported PVC blinds can be stabilised with lead, which forms a fine dust on the surface as the plastic ages in sunlight. Non-PVC blinds avoid it entirely.

name: Air-Conditioner & HVAC Mould
context: Mould growing on damp cooling coils and filters, then circulated
swap: Regular filter changes, coil cleaning and fixing condensation
note: Damp air-handling equipment can grow mould whose spores are then blown through the home. Routine maintenance and controlling moisture keep it from spreading.

name: In-Tank Toilet Cleaner Tablets
context: Chlorine-releasing tablets sitting in the toilet cistern
swap: A brush plus vinegar or an as-needed bowl cleaner
note: In-tank tablets slowly release chlorine chemicals into standing water and the bathroom air. Manual cleaning as needed avoids a constant low-level release.

name: Aerosol Oven Cleaner (Lye Fumes)
context: Caustic spray oven cleaner used in an enclosed kitchen
swap: A baking-soda paste left overnight, then wiped
note: Spray oven cleaners atomise sodium hydroxide and solvents that are corrosive to airways. A baking-soda paste does the same job without the caustic mist.

name: Chemical Drain Cleaner
context: Lye- or acid-based liquid drain openers
swap: A drain snake, plunger or enzyme-based opener
note: Strong chemical drain cleaners are highly corrosive and can release fumes or splash. Mechanical tools and enzyme products clear most clogs without the hazard.

name: Fabric & Upholstery Stain Cleaner
context: Solvent-based spot cleaners for carpets and sofas
swap: Water-based cleaners or a DIY vinegar solution
note: Many spot cleaners rely on volatile solvents and sometimes fluorinated repellents that linger in soft furnishings. Water-based options cut the residual off-gassing.

name: Cigarette Smoking (Firsthand)
context: Directly inhaling tobacco combustion products
swap: Evidence-based cessation support and nicotine-replacement
note: Firsthand tobacco smoke is one of the largest avoidable exposures there is, delivering thousands of toxicants including known carcinogens. Cessation services meaningfully improve the odds of quitting.

name: Charcoal Grill Briquettes (PAH Smoke)
context: Fat dripping onto hot charcoal, coating food in smoke
swap: Lump charcoal or gas, and avoid charring the food
note: Flare-ups and heavy smoke deposit polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons on grilled food. Lower heat, trimming fat and avoiding charring reduce how much forms.

name: Gas-Powered Leaf Blower (2-Stroke)
context: Standing behind a two-stroke engine that burns oil with fuel
swap: A battery-electric leaf blower
note: Two-stroke engines burn a fuel-oil mix inefficiently, producing high levels of unburned hydrocarbons and fine particles right at head height. Battery models eliminate the exhaust.

name: Fireworks Smoke (Perchlorate & Metals)
context: Standing downwind of consumer fireworks
swap: Watch from a distance, upwind
note: Firework smoke carries perchlorate and metal particulates that briefly spike local air pollution. Watching from upwind and at a distance limits what you inhale.

name: Hookah / Shisha Smoke
context: Water-pipe tobacco smoked over a long session
swap: Avoiding it — the water does not make it safe
note: A hookah session can deliver more smoke, carbon monoxide and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons than a single cigarette. The water pipe cools the smoke but does not filter out the toxicants.

name: Engineered Stone Countertop Dust
context: Dry-cutting or drilling quartz countertops during a fit-out
swap: Slabs cut off-site, or wet-cutting with on-tool dust extraction
note: Engineered 'quartz' stone is typically over 90% crystalline silica, against 40–50% for granite. Dry-cutting it releases respirable silica that permanently scars the lungs; hundreds of silicosis cases have been counted among fabricators. Householders are barely exposed unless a slab is dry-cut indoors.

name: Methylene Chloride Paint Stripper
context: Solvent paint and coating removers used in a closed room
swap: A benzyl-alcohol or soy-based stripper, or sanding with dust extraction
note: Methylene chloride vapour displaces oxygen in the blood and has killed people refinishing bathtubs in unventilated spaces. US regulators banned it from consumer paint and coating removal in 2019 and tightened the remaining uses under a 2024 risk-management rule.

name: Coal-Tar Driveway Sealant (PAHs)
context: Black sealer coating a drive, path or parking lot
swap: An asphalt-based sealer, or leaving the surface unsealed
note: Coal-tar sealcoat is loaded with polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons. Worn particles track indoors on shoes and tyres: US Geological Survey sampling found PAH in house dust about 25 times higher in homes beside coal-tar-sealed lots than beside plain asphalt or concrete.

name: Ozone-Generating Air Purifiers
context: 'Ionic' or ozone air cleaners run in an occupied room
swap: A true-HEPA purifier with activated carbon, and open windows
note: Ozone is a lung irritant, and the EPA's review concluded these devices do not control indoor pollutants effectively at concentrations that stay below public-health limits. Some ionisers also make ozone as a by-product, then sell the resulting smell as 'fresh air' when it is the irritant itself.

name: Vermiculite Attic Insulation (Asbestos)
context: Loose grey-brown pebble insulation in a pre-1990 attic
swap: Leaving it sealed and undisturbed; an accredited asbestos contractor if it must move
note: A single Montana mine supplied over 70% of US vermiculite between 1919 and 1990 and its ore was contaminated with asbestos, so vermiculite loft insulation from that era — often sold as Zonolite — should be assumed to contain it. Undisturbed it releases little; disturbing it during DIY is the risk.

name: Titanium Dioxide (E171) in Food
context: A white colourant in sweets, icing, sauces and supplements
swap: Products with no 'titanium dioxide' or 'E171' on the ingredient list
note: In 2021 the European food-safety regulator concluded E171 can no longer be considered safe as a food additive, because genotoxicity could not be ruled out and the particles accumulate slowly in the body. The EU withdrew it from food; it is still permitted in the US, so labels are worth reading.

name: Red Dye No. 3 (Erythrosine)
context: A bright cherry-red synthetic colour in sweets and drinks
swap: Colour from beetroot, paprika extract or carmine
note: The US regulator revoked its authorisation in January 2025 — as a point of law, not of demonstrated human harm. The Delaney Clause forbids any additive that causes cancer in animals, and the agency stated plainly that the rat mechanism involved does not occur in people. A low priority next to real exposures.

name: Brominated Vegetable Oil (Citrus Sodas)
context: A flavour stabiliser in some citrus-flavoured soft drinks
swap: Sparkling water with fresh citrus, or any soda not listing BVO
note: BVO kept citrus flavouring from separating out, at up to 15 parts per million. In July 2024 the US regulator revoked the authorisation after studies run with the NIH found the potential for adverse effects in humans; bromine accumulates in fat. Most drinks makers had already reformulated.

name: Parabens in Cosmetics
context: Preservatives in lotions, shampoos and make-up
swap: Products preserved with phenoxyethanol or sodium benzoate
note: The longer-chain parabens are the ones regulators acted on: the EU caps propyl- and butylparaben at 0.14% and bars them from leave-on nappy-area products for under-threes, on weak oestrogenic-activity grounds. Methyl- and ethylparaben are better tolerated and still permitted at higher levels.

name: Homosalate Sunscreen
context: A chemical UV filter in daily face and body sunscreen
swap: A mineral zinc-oxide sunscreen, or a filter such as Tinosorb
note: After an EU scientific committee flagged possible endocrine activity, the permitted level was cut from 10% to 7.34% and restricted to face products. It is still allowed at 10% elsewhere, including the US. Do not stop using sunscreen over this — change the filter instead.

name: Locally Caught Freshwater Fish
context: Fish taken from local rivers and lakes rather than bought
swap: Check your state, Tribal or territory fish advisory before eating the catch
note: In July 2024 the EPA added twelve PFAS to the contaminants it recommends states and Tribes monitor in locally caught freshwater fish, and says its national fish-tissue survey has found PFAS at levels that may affect health. Advisories are issued water by water, so which lake or river the fish came from matters more than the species.

name: Sewage-Sludge Fertiliser on Garden Soil
context: Biosolids spread or sold as a soil conditioner or fertiliser
swap: A soil amendment whose feedstock is stated on the bag, or compost you make yourself
note: The EPA released a draft risk assessment on 14 January 2025 covering PFOA and PFOS in sewage sludge that is land-applied as a soil conditioner or fertiliser. It is a draft that went out for public comment, not a rule, so the useful response is knowing what an amendment is made from rather than treating any number as settled.

name: Fluorinated Plastic Containers
context: Fluorine-treated HDPE bottles holding household and garden liquids
swap: The same product in an untreated container; ask the maker whether the bottle is fluorinated
note: Treating a plastic bottle with fluorine to stop it leaking or swelling can form PFAS on the inner wall. EPA testing detected eight PFAS in rinsate from fluorinated HDPE containers at 20 to 50 parts per billion, and its September 2022 study found they leach into the liquid stored inside and keep leaching the longer it sits. The EPA says such containers are used for household consumer, pesticide, fuel and automotive products.

name: Dairy from PFAS-Affected Farmland
context: Milk and dairy from livestock grazing land carrying PFAS
swap: Where a local advisory names affected farms, dairy sourced outside that area
note: The EPA lists dairy products from livestock exposed to PFAS among the routes by which PFAS reach food, alongside fish from contaminated water, and notes that biosolids used on agricultural land can affect animals that graze it. The pathway runs through the land, so it surfaces near known contamination rather than everywhere.
